abstract: The decay exponent $α$ in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as $s_i = A_i \cdot (t-i)^{-α}$, where $A_i$ is cumulative attention and $α$ controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to $α=0$ and $α\to\infty$, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of \citet{xiang2026nohair} bounds the admissible range of $α$, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields $[0.556, 0.822]$ for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. \textsc{NoHairCache} achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM ($p < 0.05$ on all three datasets, with $0.06$--$0.10$ PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget $512$). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining $98.2\%$ of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at $25\%$ retention versus $91.1\%$ for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.
